speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister, who yesterday misinformed the House in replying to a question asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. He said, when discussing the problem of poverty in Canada, that what is important is that the group of Canadians below the poverty line be reduced, and he maintained that the statistics he gave in Calgary bore this out.
Mr. Speaker, the statistics presented by his Minister of National Health and Welfare, and Statistics Canada, simply do not bear him out. I would ask whether he will today admit that the totally inaccurate claim which he made in western Canada before a Liberal convention, that the number of those living below the poverty level in Canada has been reduced from 20 per cent to 10 per cent, was achieved by ludicrously assuming that the dollar level of poverty in 1961 ought to be applied in 1975, thus totally ignoring the effects of inflation which all honest presentations of such figures take into account?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: PAYMENT UNDER WESTERN GRAIN STABILIZATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to announce to the House today that an initial payment of $60 million has been approved under the western grain stabilization program.
April 5, 1978

Western Grain Stabilization Payment
Producers who have paid the $500 maximum levy over each of the past two years will be getting about $1,100 as a part payment for the 1977 crop. A final payment will be made in the fall when all the information needed to determine the final pay-out level under the act has been gathered. Right now it looks as if that final payment will also be a pretty hefty one.
This part payment will help grain growers meet planting expenses for the coming year. The purpose of setting up the Western Grain Stabilization Act on a calendar basis was to allow producers this type of flexible assistance. I understand that cheques will be going out very shortly. In fact, producers can expect to have them in their hands by the end of April. This should be of considerable help to prairie grain farmers particularly, in view of the decreased net returns prairie farmers suffered last year.

subtopic: PAYMENT UNDER WESTERN GRAIN STABILIZATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we on this side welcome this announcement by the minister for two reasons. First, the announcement was mercifully short and, second, the money is badly needed now. The announcement emphasizes the problem facing the western grain industry, which is really just a reflection of the total problem facing Canadian agriculture.
This announcement is one more indicator that an election is imminent. Yesterday in the Standing Committee on Agriculture the minister said this announcement could not be made until after the cabinet meeting tomorrow, so he is either talking through his hat or he does not understand cabinet procedure, or both.
We are now 30 million bushels behind in our grain exports, mainly because of problems at the west coast. Farmers know that the asking price for top grade grain is $4.50 a bushel plus, but still the government says there will be no further payment on the initial price of $2.75 a bushel received by the farmer. For those people this announcement today will be small comfort. It means that they are sold out at below the cost of production for the full calendar year 1978.
At a time when close to $1 billion will have to be expended to plant the prairie grain crop, which requires seed, fuel, chemicals, equipment and wages, producers will question why this payment could not be made in full instead of in two parts. The money is required now. The fund presently has in it $154 million, give or take $1 million or $2 million. The $60 million payment announced by the minister today is simply a return of the premiums already paid by farmers, and if the government honestly feels that the western grain stabilization plan is so great, why does it not include landlords? By "landlords" I mean mainly widows who live in our small prairie towns. These are the people who are being hurt. I sincerely hope that in the coming years returns from the marketplace will preclude payments of this kind.

subtopic: PAYMENT UNDER WESTERN GRAIN STABILIZATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the spokesman for the Conservative party, we in the NDP welcome the fact that farmers are getting some additional moneys, but I must admit that I am not really surprised at the announcement. It is really an election payment which is being

made to the farmers. Farmers are being paid $1,100, as a maximum, of their own money, and if we look at the plan, we find that over the last two years farmers contributed $1,000, $500 per year. If we add interest, that amounts to $1,100, so they are getting back their own money. I think this is a bit of cynical politics on the part of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan).
The announcement today says that a final payment will be made in the fall when all the information needed to determine the final pay-out under the act has been gathered. Of course, we will not have that information in the fall. I suppose it is by accident that there is an initial payment. We welcome that initial payment, but I want to be sure that this is a precedent, and in other than election years when there is a pay-out under the plan there had better be an initial payment like there is this year. It had better not be just in an election year that the government decides to pay farmers with their own money in an attempt to buy votes. I want to be sure that the minister uses this as a precedent.
I do not think the Minister of Agriculture knows very much about this because his boss is out in Saskatchewan making a similar announcement today.

speechtext: Winnipeg.

subtopic: PAYMENT UNDER WESTERN GRAIN STABILIZATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
By his "boss" I mean the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, who is announcing that there will be a hefty payment in the fall. If the government can project a hefty payment in the fall, why can that payment not be made now? It would make more sense to make the payment now than it would in the fall.
The minister who made this announcement in the House today is full of nothing but bull when he talks about the decent farm incomes we have in this country. Net farm incomes in the last three years have dropped by 23 per cent. Farm expenses have gone up by 18 per cent. Is that the best there is in the world? When the minister cannot answer questions in the House, he pats himself on the back, and he spreads a bunch of bull from one end of the country to the other.
In my province of Saskatchewan between 1975 and 1977 cash receipts for grain and oil seeds went down by 20 per cent, while the cost to the farmer went up by some 23 per cent. Some Minister of Agriculture and some department!
Between January, 1975 and January, 1978 cash receipts for farmers went down by 38 per cent, and in the province of Saskatchewan they went down 55 per cent. What other sector of our economy would sit back quietly and allow that to happen? The minister announced nothing today for beef producers. All he has announced is a measly payment out of the western grain stabilization fund, money which the farmers themselves have put into it. Of course we welcome the payment, but it is not enough. If farmers are going to stay in business, they will need a lot more than this.

subtopic: PAYMENT UNDER WESTERN GRAIN STABILIZATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment very briefly on the statement the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) just made on western Canada's grain growers.
That the government decided to extend financial aid to farmers can only be good news, whether those farmers are in western, central or eastern Canada. Because it is generally recognized by members in this Elouse that farm producers are finding it very difficult to gain recognition for their right to a reasonable and stable return, bad seasons and bad years notwithstanding.
As far as I am concerned, I know western grain growers are facing difficulties, and the announcement that an initial $60 million payment has been approved will be welcome because those farmers have obligations and any revenue will allow them to honour those obligations, at least in part, and provide them with some incentive to consider the coming crop year and the seeding season with better hope and satisfaction.
On the other hand, it is too bad farmers have to wait for months on end before at least recouping the money they spent on seeding, maintenance, threshing, storage and so forth, and still wait another number of months before getting a revenue, some return on their labour. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that through the years it will be possible to develop a program ensuring better stability, so that our country can produce on a regular basis what is needed to feed this country and also to meet our commitments to the underdeveloped countries we are helping generously.
I am happy about this, about the fact that we can help because, in my opinion, it is more satisfying to help others then to have to ask others for help. While the Minister of Agriculture is still in his seat, 1 would like to make a small comment concerning the Canadian dairy producers.
Yesterday, when I asked the minister about this, he replied that we would be proud when he announces the dairy policy for next year and that we would be happy to learn that we have the best dairy policy in the world. If it really is the best in the world, 1 shall be the first to applaud. When someone does something positive, something which truly corresponds with the aspirations of a group of Canadian producers, I am not one to criticize, as I would rather help with the administration and co-operate, and on those occasions, 1 am happy and proud to say that such a thing is good.
Therefore, in the days to come, 1 hope the Minister of Agriculture will tell us about the nature of this dairy policy to reassure the Canadian dairy producers so that they will also start the next dairy production year in good spirits and work generously like all other producers of western Canada to produce the goods essential for Canada.
Western Grain Stabilization Payment
Mr. Speaker, if this is the situation, the member for Bellechasse will be happy to say so throughout Canada and invite all our producers to take advantage of this policy and to continue to work generously to accomplish their mission, and we shall assure them of our support to provide them with reasonable returns and to ensure the future of agriculture in Canada, which is essential for the survival and the prosperity of our country.

Standing Orders
$2. It will be that kind of program. This is a voluntary program. The farmers are not forced to join. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the notice I sent you earlier today I wish to ask leave to move the adjournment of this House, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 26, for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely the shattering of world confidence in our economy as evidenced by the selling off of Canada's April 1 bond issue in New York, the arrangement of a further emergency credit of $1 billion from our Canadian chartered banks, the imploring by our Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) that our provinces, municipalities and corporations borrow more actively in foreign markets, only to be countered by the reported statement by the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais) in Sarnia yesterday that "international debt is caused by Canadian businesses borrowing on the international market" which he felt was bad.
The urgency of this matter has been aggravated by the refusal of the Minister of Finance to come before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs for the next two weeks, notwithstanding the fact that he has not appeared once on his main estimates for this year.

Nevertheless, the matter itself is the shattering of world confidence in our economy, which is an opinion rather than an event. 1 do not make a final determination on that, but it seems to me that the language of the Standing Order does not really lend itself readily to a debate of an opinion, as it does to the consideration of a specific event. However, I say again that I do not make that as a final determination. That could be subject to argument and in certain circumstances it may be applicable. I do not think it is here.

Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), in which he was joined by the hon. leader of the New Democratic party (Mr. Broad-bent). As I say, 1 might be persuaded otherwise in that regard.
The third reason, which 1 think involves the final determination, is that in answer to questions this week the Minister of Finance has indicated, and he did so again today in answer to a question, that after tomorrow's cabinet meeting he will be giving an indication about the presentation of a budget. 1 really think I would have to overlook entirely the provisions of paragraph (5) of the Standing Order if I did not at least wait to see whether such a budget is to be presented. I say that because I think that the minister can be faulted virtually on all fronts. He refused to answer a question today when I asked him this: In view of the fact that unemployment has risen since he has taken office last September-inflation has risen, his deficit has widened, the dollar has fallen-does he feel he has done anything wrong? Normally, I would have expected him to get to his feet and clarify the situation or defend himself. However, the nature of the question shocked him so much that he sat dumbfounded, realizing I had hit upon the truth.
The Minister of Finance has made some serious mistakes. International financial circles are able to identify almost within the hour when mistakes have been made by this minister. These mistakes have helped to shatter the Canadian economic image throughout the world and resulted in the further decline-of our dollar. This is due to the minister's presentation and lack of comprehension of the nature of this job. In short, he has bumbled, but unfortunately he is not the one who suffers most. It is the Canadian public that are suffering from his want of knowledge in a department that is so vital to Canada's wellbeing today.
In saying that, and in dealing with the question of inflation under Bill C-18, we must bear in mind that one of the contributing reasons for the decline of our dollar is that the international banking world is judging us as an inflation-prone nation when other nations have been able to get control of their inflation. They find that Canada has become a stand-out nation where inflation continues to rise. As we said on Monday, it has risen by 9.5 per cent. It continues to rise much faster than it has been rising in the United States and is almost triple the rate in Germany. Switzerland has no inflation.
We are told by this Minister of Finance, backed up by his emperor overlord, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), that they do not know what to do to control inflation in this country. In my opening, rather brief preliminary remarks last Monday, Mr. Speaker-I see the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance is laughing. Frankly, the question of our economic condition in Canada at the present time is not a laughing matter.
In the opening remarks I made last Monday I pointed out, for example, that the outflow from our foreign exchange reserves was costing Canadians dearly. It is easy to forget that on August 31 last year, about six months ago, United States reserves held on behalf of the Canadian public by the Bank of Canada were $2,558 million. Since that time and with the arrival of the Minister of Finance in September to take over the reins of finance in this country, we have had a deterioration in those reserves of $1.6 billion. If you add the outflow of United States reserves so far in April alone-Monday, Tuesday and today-there has probably been $1.7 to $1.8 billion lost with respect to the United States reserves that we held

when this Minister of Finance took over the reins on behalf of the Government of Canada.
If you translate that into more meaningful terms, it means that the ineptitude and lack of comprehension shown by the Minister of Finance has cost the average taxpayer in Canada $180 of the United States reserves that he rightfully could have expected to be maintained by the Bank of Canada on his behalf. It has cost every taxpayer in Canada $180.
Let me put that into perspective. When we are talking in terms of billions of dollars-and frankly most of us, including myself, cannot comprehend what a billion dollars is-let us not forget that our reserves have now dwindled to the point where we, in relation to our external obligations, be they of a debt nature or trade nature, have the thinnest reserves of any industrialized nation in the world. In that context it is not too hard to understand why the international community has the jitters about Canada when they see our reserves are so thin and they observe the bumbling, stumbling actions of this government. When the international community sees the half measures the government brings in in order to try to counter the lack of confidence that there is in the system, it is not hard to understand why the run on the Canadian dollar continues. The obvious reason why the run continues is that the government's program to counter inflation in this country has failed.
That is why, when dealing with Bill C-18, I think it wise to continue to press this government for an explanation of why the program they enunciated on October 20, 1975 to help fight inflation in this country was not carried out. If you recall, Mr. Speaker, the program was quite explicit. It said the government was going to make some basic changes in the way they were running the country. They were going to be restrained in their own fiscal spending. They were going to be restrained in their monetary growth. They were going to start deregulating industry and set up a controls mechanism through the AntiInflation Board that somehow would keep the lid on prices, profits and wages in the country.
I think the time has come to ask the government what went wrong with the program that they told the Canadian people, and certainly this parliament, they intended to follow. Certainly we do not have the fiscal restraint. Anybody who wishes to attend the committees of this House and review the estimates now before us-the $50 billion spending that the government contemplates for the coming year-realizes there is no fiscal restraint. We have not had the monetary restraint referred to in October of 1975, we have not had the deregulation referred to, and, of course, the controls that were presumably supposed to keep the lid on the rising prices, profits and wages have not worked either.
I ask what went wrong because we must not forget that the targets the government set for themselves were, if anything, high targets. When they said we would be getting down to 4 per cent inflation this year, that was not only an attainable goal if we had been in power in 1975, it was a high goal. If Germany got inflation down to 3.5 per cent this year compared
April 5, 1978

to our 9.5 per cent, then I must ask this government why they cannot do the same. If Switzerland can get down to zero inflation at the present time compared to our 9.5 per cent, then I ask this government why they cannot.
The hard fact is that this government does not have to live with some of the problems a country like Switzerland has. Other than salt, basically Switzerland has no resources whatsoever. They have to import practically everything they need. That is not our situation, Mr. Speaker. We are virtually self-sufficient in energy, we are virtually self-sufficient in such resources as nickel, iron and other minerals and we are rich in agricultural products. In short, of all industrialized nations, we have fewer problems than others. Switzerland, Germany and Japan, for instance, have very, very serious problems but in spite of them have been able to handle their level of inflation in a much more satisfactory way.
The figures I used are on the record, Mr. Speaker. I shall not take hon. members through the Bank of Canada's February 1970 Review again. It points out the comparative position as far as consumer prices are concerned in the various countries listed. We must not forget, however, that the Bank of Canada-and few members will want to dispute what the Bank of Canada says in this regard-points out that in December, 1977, the 12-month inflation level in the United States was 6.8 per cent compared to the Canadian 9.5 per cent; the Japanese inflation rate was 4.9 per cent compared to our 9.5 per cent; and the German rate was 3.5 per cent compared to our 9.5 per cent. In fact, all those major industrialized countries were lumped together and 7.2 per cent is the average inflation level compared to our 9.5 per cent. I think those Bank of Canada figures are a sad testimony to the effective management of our economy by this government.
Toward the end of my opening remarks on Monday, Mr. Speaker, I said that I should like to deal with the historical perspective of this question. I hear the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lumley) suggesting that I should shorten my remarks. I find it not only reprehensible that the government does not have the courage to tell the people of Canada what they believe the facts to be, but that they seem to have absolute disdain for anybody in this House who tries to enter the debate of the day as it should be debated.

I should like to return to my concluding remarks when I spoke on Monday concerning Bill C-18, Mr. Speaker. I feel it is proper to put into historical perspective what "the Trudeau government role" has been on this whole question. Let us not forget that a large proportion of the money printed in recent years by the Bank of Canada has gone to finance the Trudeau government's deficits. For the members of this House who were not here Monday night when I dealt with this question of the creation of inflation by the over-printing of money in relation to the real growth in the economy, I would reiterate that that is the basic cause of inflation in any nation.
As I pointed out, during the ten years of mismanagement by the Trudeau emperor, we have had money created to the extent of 156 per cent in this country. During that same period of approximately ten years the real growth in the economy, Mr. Speaker, was 55 per cent. Is it any wonder that we had 100 per cent inflation during the present government's tenure

April 5, 1978
Anti-Inflation Act
of office since 1968? These are the facts. Basically, let us not forget the more people pretend that they do not know-and certain politicians pretend that they do not know what causes inflation-the more they are not being fair to the Canadian public. Inflation basically cannot be caused in a nation unless more money is printed than the real growth of the economy permits.
That is why I come back to this question of the nature of the printing of money by the Bank of Canada. The fact is the Bank of Canada printed money to finance 33 per cent of the federal cash requirements needed by this government in the past five years. The $5.6 billion of federal securities purchased by the Bank of Canada represents more than 60 per cent of the total addition to the money supply over the period I am referring to.
Let us bear in mind that when the Prime Minister took the reins of power, when he became the senior executive in this country, the total federal securities owned by the Bank of Canada were approximately $4 billion. Since that time securities owned by the bank have risen to almost $11 billion. That increase from $4 billion to $11 billion is what people mean by monetarizing the debt of the nation. When the debt of the nation is monetarized, that is the classic way to print more money; more money is flushed into the system which causes the inflation we are now living with. I cannot dwell on that point too often because it is the point that every government in power which acts irresponsibly with respect to the management of the economy likes to forget. The main cause of inflation occurs when governments over-print money in relation to real growth. The terrible culprit in Canada has been the present administration.
The spending practices of the present government created the budgetary deficits which where partially financed by increasing the money supply, as I have indicated. Since 1968 federal spending has more than quadrupled. If the $50 billion figure is accepted, it is up almost five times. In 1968 the federal government announced preliminary federal spending intentions of $10.9 billion. In 1979, using the government's own figures, it will be $46.5 billion, which is the figure I am referring to when I say there has been approximately a fourfold increase in government spending.
Before I go further, Mr. Speaker, let us make a quick review of the present administration's strategy against inflation. First of all are the years 1973 to 1975. Early in 1973 it became apparent that the administration had not licked inflation as the Prime Minister was wont to claim. In 1971 we find that the rate of inflation was approaching 6 per cent. It was showing no signs of lessening since the money supply was growing in excess of 15 per cent. In short, the return of inflation in that period was not surprising.
In the budget of February, 1973, the present administration stated that fiscal measures were, and I quote, "aimed at reducing inflationary pressures in Canada". The strategy was to increase supply, to increase disposable incomes, to protect Canadians against inflation and to restrict federal government demands upon the economy. In many ways, are not those

familiar terms even today? Wage and price controls were flatly rejected in that budget.
That strategy, of course, was a failure. Inflation which stood at 5.8 per cent reached 9.6 per cent a year later, and was still rising. The strategy might have had more effect if it had been properly implemented. Where smaller federal demands upon the economy were promised, federal spending actually grew 23 per cent in the following year. Let us not forget that figure.
In spite of the fact that in the February, 1973 budget we were told that the government was at last going to restrain their spending, in the very next year they increased it by 23 per cent. By the next budget, in May, 1974, inflation had reached 11 per cent and was still rising. The budget reflected to use the government's words, "determination to deal with inflation." Lip service to spending restraint was dropped. Federal spending grew at the even faster rate that year of 28 per cent. Once again the present administration rejected the illusory magic, as they called it, of controls. During the subsequent election campaign-how well we all remember- the Prime Minister called controls "a proven disaster looking for a new place to happen". At the same time he pledged his government, and I quote again, "to bring inflation under control." That was the Prime Minister's pledge to the people of Canada which presumably influenced them in voting for his re-election in 1974.
With the rate of inflation approaching 12 per cent the then finance minister, Mr. Turner, prescribed the same medicine once again in November 1974 that he had been prescribing previously and unfortunately it had the same effect. The inflation rate was hovering around 11 per cent when he presented his last budget in June 1975. The principal measure was, again, promised restraint in federal spending. While the present administration claimed it had cut $1 billion from federal spending plans, federal spending was still forecast to increase by an alarming 11 per cent over the year before. That, Mr. Speaker, is a very brief summary of what the government said and did during the 1973 to 1975 period.
Let us take a look at 1975 through to 1978 and at what brings us to the debate on Bill C-18 at the present time. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that by October 1975 the inflation rate was still in excess of 10 per cent. After nearly three years of budgets directed against inflation, three years during which the government had consistently rejected the use of wage and price controls, the present government introduced the antiinflation program, which I have referred to. The central component of it was none other than wage and price controls.
At this point I should explain something. Most of us will recall that the minister of finance who presided over the economic affairs of this country during the tremendous spending binge which occurred was none other than Mr. John Turner. But Mr. Turner presumably had a falling out with the Prime Minister in that the Prime Minister was a controls-ori-ented person. He liked the sound of controls. The falling out resulted in Mr. Turner resigning and Mr. Macdonald being brought in to do the dirty work of imposing controls.
April 5, 1978

It is interesting to note that there was a change of ministers at that time. But not only was there a change of ministers. As we know, the deputy finance minister during most of the time Mr. Turner was minister of finance also resigned, and he has since stated in unequivocal terms that the inflation problem with which we are confronted today was contributed to in large measure by the overspending of the federal government during the Turner years. That is a little of the background.
Then we find that the anti-inflation program of October, 1975 proposed to reduce inflation from its level of 10.6 per cent to 4 per cent by October, 1978. As I said earlier, that 4 per cent target was not an overly high one. It was relatively realistic. The anti-inflation program also promised that federal spending would be restrained, that the growth in the money supply would be greatly restricted, that there would be "a review with some urgency of the federal government's responsibility for creating price rigidities in its own area of responsibility", and that there would be a reassessment of the cost to the private sector of government rules and regulations. Finally, a review of the role of regulatory agencies was to be undertaken.
The promise of federal spending restraint, Mr. Speaker, has not been kept. Over the two years of so-called restraint the estimates of federal spending have risen by 28 per cent, and those increases have occurred due to the administration's own internal operating costs. Let no hon. member forget this. During the two years of so-called restraint, operating costs have increased by 37 per cent. That, Mr. Speaker, is the government in action. That, if you like, is charisma in action for the Canadian public to enjoy. The cost to the taxpayer has been horrendous. If the cost of federal operations had run parallel to the inflation guidelines of the control period, federal expenditures would today be $2 billion lower than they are.
Let us remember, also, that the growth of the money supply has been held within the limits proposed by the Bank of Canada primarily because the targets were so generous. The first set of targets called for money supply growth amounting to between 10 per cent and 15 per cent effective September, 1975. The second set called for growth rates between 8 per cent and 12 per cent effective March, 1976, and the third set for rates between 7 per cent and 11 per cent effective last June. These targets all represent rates of monetary expansion which are not consistent with price stability. They are an improvement in relation to previous performance but they are still, in our opinion, too high.
Throughout most of the controls program monetary expansion has been below the target range. Recently, however, the money supply has been growing at much higher rates. In December, 1977 the money supply was 12 per cent higher than in December, 1976, a rate of expansion higher than the target range. If such growth continues, the Bank of Canada will slip back into an inflationary posture not much different from that which created the initial problem.
The administration has given us no indication that it is reviewing the contribution to inflation made by federal agen-
Anti-Inflation Act
cies. Indeed, the federal government has specifically exempted a number of Crown corporations and agencies from the application of its own price and profit control guidelines. Such an action clearly indicates that the administration does not view the activities of its own agencies as being in any way inflationary.
Further, the government has published no studies and offered no initiatives relating to its commitment to reassess the economic costs of federal regulations. Recently the minister of state responsible for small business announced he would establish a program to reduce the paperwork burden on small business. The first step, Mr. Speaker, is to be a study. Guess of what. A study of what the problem is. More than two years after a commitment is made to reduce the regulatory burden, the present administration has progressed as far as studying the problem. In order to do so they intend to appoint, they say, a comptroller of the paper burden, with a staff of 20.

speechtext:
If it were not so sad it would be almost laughable to compare the rhetoric of the government with its actions. There has been no indication that the government is reviewing or has reviewed the role of its regulatory agencies. Ministers have admitted publicly that they do not know how many Crown corporations the government owns; the total is over 385 and they are still counting. It is unlikely the administration will be able to accomplish the review it promised even if all the regulatory agencies can be identified. New regulatory agencies are still being created; for example, there is the national broiler board, the Northern Pipeline Agency, the competition policy advocate and, of course, the comptroller of the paper burden.
Let me add one almost humorous note. Here we are dealing with Bill C-18, which proposes to amend the anti-inflation legislation. The government, according to the Financial Post this week, has given an assurance to the 700-man staff of the AIB that they will be shifted to other government jobs should the board ever be dismantled. Here is a government which created an agency, one which it told us would never be established, and then announced that the number on the staff would not be more than 200 temporary employees. Now we find the board has a staff of 700, and when it is suggested the board might be dismantled the employees are assured they will never be allowed to drift away from the public service but will be guaranteed jobs at salaries comparable with those they now receive under the AIB.
Let me now deal with the lack of success-indeed, I might say the failure-of controls. Since the present administration has been unwilling to honour its commitments on spending restraint, monetary restraint, and the proliferation of bureaucracy, it is not surprising that wage and price controls have been unable to slow inflation. In fact, the failure of this administration to implement supportive policies has made controls virtually irrelevant in the anti-inflation campaign.

April 5, 1978
Anti-Inflation Act
Wage controls, for example, did not halt the erosion of our competitive trade position with the United States. Studies by the Conference Board of Canada indicate that the deterioration in our competitive position has continued throughout the controls program. All the devaluation of the Canadian dollar has done is restore our competitive position to what it was in 1975 when our competitive position was so poor that controls were required.
On the question of the effect of a declining dollar hon. members will recall that this party initially pointed out to the government that a falling dollar is not a mixed blessing. The government was saying that the fall in the dollar would help exports, but we were pointing out that it would also trigger a new round of inflation in the country. As the Conference Board pointed out in the quote to which 1 referred, the fact is that the devaluation which had occurred up to the date of the report simply had put us back to the competitive position we were in in 1975, the very year the government said it had to bring in controls because we had lost our competitive position in relation to the rest of the world.
The important thing to bear in mind now is that the government at last seems to be coming to its senses. It is realizing that the falling dollar is in fact generating its own inflation, and we now find that the Governor of the Bank of Canada in a release dated April 3 stated that, and 1 quote:
-too large an exchange rate adjustment over too short a period of time would not be helpful in restoring Canada's international competitive position on a durable basis because of the risk that it would undermine the substantial progress Canada has made to date in overcoming inflation.
In short, the economy is in a tailspin. The government has allowed the dollar to drift lower, and to the degree that it has allowed the dollar to drift lower it is in turn generating inflation about which even the governor of the Bank of Canada has become alarmed.
Let me touch on another point. In our opinion the price and profit controls imposed on the nation through the government's anti-inflation program were quite an unnecessary burden on the business community. Corporate profits have been so sluggish that in 1976 only 20 per cent of the firms subject to profit controls had been within 10 per cent of the allowable maximum profit. Most firms had such small profits that the profit restraints were unnecessary. In 1976 Canadian business was generating only 51 per cent of the maximum profit allowable under very strict profit restraining guidelines. The steadily worsening economic situation has narrowed business profit margins independently of controls. Profit margins of industrial corporations had already fallen from 1974 levels of 7.2 per cent to the level of 6.1 per cent in the nine months of 1975 before controls were introduced. Margins fell further in 1976 to 5.2 per cent and declined to 5.1 per cent in 1977.
Wage controls, on the other hand, did not halt the erosion of our competitive position, nor were profit controls necessary in the current economic circumstances. The costs of controls have been huge. Labour-management relations have been damaged severely by prolonged federal intervention. Business confidence and investment are low. These costs might have been sustain-

able if inflation had fallen to forecast levels, but as we have pointed out, inflation has not come down to the 4 per cent target. Where the inflation rate was originally forecast to be in the 4 per cent to 6 per cent range at this time, as we know the rate is now 9.5 per cent. The Trudeau government's controls have failed. Not only have they failed, but they have produced the costs to which I have referred which have had to be borne by business. Let me put this into perspective. One corporation has told me that its cost for staff and administration simply to cope with the anti-inflation program is $500,000 a year.
What are the new policies enunciated by this administration to fight inflation? The government now says that the phase-out of the disastrous controls program will begin on April 14 of this year. However, as I indicated on Monday, 70 per cent of workers and 80 per cent of companies will remain under controls until the end of 1978. Even after the expiry of controls certain rules and guidelines will continue to apply. Monitoring of prices and wages in the post-controls period is now to be undertaken by the Economic Council of Canada. Whatever group does the monitoring will be a watchdog, without real powers.
We are told that inflation will reach 6 per cent in 1978. Hon. members will recall that at the first ministers' conference the government forecast an inflation rate of 3.5 per cent by 1982, but no policies have been implemented or even proposed to move Canada from the current 8 per cent plus inflation level to the 3.5 per cent level the government claims can be achieved by 1982. Let me be candid on that. We believe that an inflation level lower than 3.5 per cent could be achieved by 1982. That is not the point. What we are saying is that it will not be achieved, any more than was the 4 per cent inflation level achieved this year, if the government does not now take the necessary steps to ensure that it will be achieved.
Repeatedly the Minister of Finance likes to maintain in his inept way that he sees nothing wrong with existing federal fiscal and monetary policies. That is most unfortunate.
Let me now deal with what we in the Progressive Conservative party think should be done in this country to reduce inflation. First of all, we should end controls, but they should not be ended in this disgraceful way by saying that there will be a decontrol period starting on April 14, but in fact keeping 70 per cent to 80 per cent of the employees and companies in this country bound up until the end of the year. We believe that, if anything, wage controls have been inflationary. What starts out as a wage ceiling over time becomes a floor for wage settlements. That is a consequence of a controls program which lasts too long.
Profit controls, no doubt, have been inflationary. They have retarded investment projects which would have protected the economy from inflation resulting from supply shortages. Profit controls have increased the burden of regulations upon business, added to cost and reduced efficiency. Profit controls have encouraged business inefficiency as a method of disposing of excess revenue.
A second thing we would do to counter inflation would be to cut income taxes. Consumers need a break. The 6 per cent
April 5, 1978

ceiling on wage gains in 1978 is inadequate to compensate workers for the inflation expected during this current year. Without a tax cut the buying power of consumers may well fall. Wage earners must be protected against inflation to avoid a catch-up explosion of wage demands in the future. We feel the tax cut should be large. It should be approximately the $2.2 billion the government is overspending at the present time. I referred to that earlier. This means that more than 1 per cent of Canada's national output, or gross national product if you like that term, will be returned to individual taxpayers; that 500,000 Canadians will be taken off the federal tax rolls if our tax cut were implemented. I say that 500,000 Canadians would be taken off our tax rolls because we recall how many ministers of finance have loved to use that term.
Not only do we feel that the tax cut would benefit the average Canadian but we believe it should be directed so as to bring the main advantages to those earning up to $16,000 a year, who would receive nearly $300 if you work out our program. In effect, we are proposing a tax cut which would give most Canadians one week's extra pay. We say that one of the problems in the economy is the lack of consumer buying. We must get the consumer buying once again, creating the demand to which the businessman will respond through additional production, and eventually the creation of more plants and the buying of more equipment to serve that demand.
If you assess the thrust of this government's stand with respect to making our economy more buoyant, Mr. Speaker, I think you can determine that they have put heavy emphasis on giving the corporate sector an incentive. But the corporate sector really needs more than an incentive; it needs the demand from the buying public to allow it to create the jobs that are so urgently needed in the country. In addition to giving the corporate sector just a blind handout incentive, one should link those incentives to productivity tests so far as those corporations are concerned, and make them work for the tax breaks they are offered through one's fiscal position. That would be part of the approach that we would adopt in bringing in a budget if we had the opportunity to do so this month.
Having said that, I should like to emphasize that timing is all important in these measures. We enunciated what I am saying in part several months ago. We urged the government to cut back on their spending and to give a more meaningful tax cut to the Canadian taxpayer. We would not have the unemployment levels today that we have if the government had taken our suggestions. But now we are saying: Although it is late, do something still; because if you do not get the economy responding in a more vigorous way, we will have higher unemployment come the winter of 1978-79.
We believe that there should be a cut in sales taxes. The federal government collects a 12 per cent sales tax on almost every purchase made by consumers. By reducing the rate of tax on particular items, for example on building materials, consumers will pay lower prices. This is a fiscal tool that could be used, if the government so wished, with precision. They can
Anti-Inflation Act
assess, for example, the hardware items that are not moving at present, the cars, refrigerators and stoves, and as the government determines where it wants to put the main thrust of its incentives, it can at least lower the sales tax, if not remove it, with respect to that particular commodity. We have referred to the manufacturers' sales tax or the federal sales tax because we feel that is a most unfortunate type of tax. It is very inflationary and it goes on products at the manufacturer level and in effect then becomes amplified as mark-ups are placed on the product between the manufacturer and the eventual end user.
Another approach that can be used is to have the provinces reduce their sales taxes. Most provinces feel that they cannot give such a cut if they do not have a break from the federal government. That is why we are saying that the federal government, and certainly the Minister of Finance, in considering the budget that he will probably bring in next week or the following week, should at least consider cutting back on taxes, or, if you like, giving a bonus to those provinces which are willing to reduce their sales tax. Surely it is most unfortunate that a province such as Newfoundland, which is experiencing the tragedy of the highest unemployment in this country, should feel it necessary to impose a 12 per cent sales tax on its goods.

The hon. member is correct. I was referring to Newfoundland having the highest unemployment rate, which is also correct. I am pointing out that it is most unfortunate that, because of lack of revenue, some of the provinces which have high unemployment-and the two things go hand in hand-have been forced to inflict upon their citizens the highest sales taxes in the country.
This is where the federal government can do something meaningful. It can make whatever compensation is needed to those provinces to allow them to start removing, or at least reducing, their sales tax so that the consumer buying enthusiasm can be restored and in turn we can get our economy working again.
The thrust of what I am saying is that if we were in power, we would get Canadians back to work. It is a disgrace that in a nation which is as bountiful as ours this government should be tolerating a real growth of only 2.6 per cent, as they did last year.
Having said those things on the revenue side, let me say where we feel those revenue items can be paid for. In short, the size of government must be reduced. By cutting back on the growth of federal spending we will reduce the contribution of the government to inflationary pressures. A variety of cuts would be made by us if we had the opportunity. The size of the federal public service would be reduced by 20,000 a year for the next three years. This would be accomplished through a hiring freeze and a policy of not replacing those who resign or retire.
In this respect we feel we should probably have to exempt prison guards, RCMP personnel and military personnel. In

short, we are simply saying that it is possible not to fill the vacancies, to let attrition of its own momentum reduce the size of our public service. If we were able to drop, say, 20,000 public servants a year through that method, this would mean about $400 million a year could be saved in spending at the federal government level.
We also feel that savings could be achieved through lower personnel support costs, lower accommodation and equipment charges, and lower transportation and communication expenditures. Again we feel that further reductions in spending could be achieved through sharply reduced advertising and consulting expenditures. One of the points we have made- certainly my leader has made them several times-is that we believe there is room for zero based budgeting and sunset laws if they were implemented by the federal government and earnestly enforced. I emphasize that because, as most of us know, the city of Hamilton has brought in a zero based approach to their budgeting. It has been tough, it has been hard to work out, but it has been successful. I think it is interesting to note that a city with a budget of approximately $100 million has been able to keep the lid on its spending to within 1 per cent of the previous year's spending. As a result of the general growth of that city, their mill rate, the actual tax rate of the homeowners in that city, has gone down this year compared to last.
Compare that city with zero based budgeting, keeping their increase to within 1 per cent of their spending last year, to this federal government which expects to receive cheers when they tell us they kept their spending approximately equal to the real growth plus inflation in the nation. They are a laugh. Hopefully the Canadian public will give them the final laugh when the election is called and the voting is recorded later this year.
We feel that some of the more than 300 Crown corporations to which I have referred should be dismantled or integrated within departments or sold to the private sector. Non-budgetary borrowings of Crown corporations should be curtailed, especially where the interest rate does not reflect market conditions.
We have before the House a bill to amend the Export Development Corporation Act in which the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) is seriously asking this House to give that one Crown corporation the right to borrow without further reference to this House, certainly of a formal nature, over $20 billion on their own account.
The Minister of Finance has said that our cash needs for fiscal year 1979 are to be $11 billion. He deliberately did not induce the borrowings of such Crown corporations as EDC because they do it in their own name. That may be so, but they bind the Government of Canada when they do it. That is clear. If you read their prospectus, Mr. Speaker, in each case across the front of it they state it is an Export Development Corporation note that you are buying, but Her Majesty the Queen in the right of Canada guarantees the note.

When we talk about cash needs, admitted by the Minister of Finance to be $ 11 billion, and we add the needs of Crown corporation such as EDC, we see how totally out of control this government is getting. If you put it into percentage terms, you find they are spending about $50 billion this year and are going to be able to pay back only 77 or 78 per cent of that spending. The rest of it is ending up on the cuff to be paid not necessarily by us, but in part, plus interest, by future generations in this country. That is why we say there has to be a cutback.
Recently some of us were in Israel. I found it most refreshing when talking to the minister of finance in Israel to hear his attitude as a new minister of finance, heading a Conservative government in that country, with regard to what they intend to do with their state corporations. The previous socialist government which ruled that country ended up with about 180 state corporations. Apparently those state corporations were into unbelievable things. They were making plastic articles, virtually anything you can conceive of, but losing money hand over fist.
When I talked to officials in their finance department, they pointed out that their country simply could not continue to subsidize the losses that were being run up by those state corporations. The solution of the new government in Israel- and this is why I say it is so refreshing-is to put on the block at least one-half of those 180 state corporations. They are simply going to ask for tenders in the private sector. If they can get suitable bids, presumably they will sell and get out of the business of running companies which no government any place in the world generally runs well.
The next point I would like to make is that we, if in power, would deregulate the economy. The burden of public bureaucracy on private enterprise must be lifted. Sunset laws will be implemented to terminate agencies which have outlived their usefulness. Tax rebates will be supplied to small businessmen who are plagued by excess federal paperwork.
We should bear in mind that the paperwork, the bureaucracy that business has to live with, is certainly an irritant to all businessmen. The large corporations handle it by simply adding to their staff. They hire another accountant or another lawyer. It is just another cost item. The small businessman cannot do that. He finds that that is often the final load that breaks him as a businessman. In short, he goes out of business.
My final point in dealing with what we would do if we were in power today is this. We feel there should be greater monetary restraint in Canada. There should be gradual reductions in the growth rate of the money supply, greater than we have been having. Monetary expansion must not be allowed to exceed growth targets that are set in relation to realistic real growth potential in this country. The federal government must put less pressure on the Bank of Canada to finance their own federal debt. The federal government must learn to live within its means.
That is our position. I believe it is a credible position. I hope it will be accepted, at least in part, by the Minister of Finance when he brings in the budget some time next week or the week
April 5, 1978

after. If he does not, let me assure him that to the extent he has cheated the Canadian public once again by taking the wrong fiscal and monetary positions in a budget, we will make it an election issue come the next election.
I have touched on the Liberal record with regard to controls.
I could touch on certain other items. I know there are other members who are anxious to get into this debate and I do not want to take an unduly long time.
