He was not being very radical, but following the advice of the Economic Council of Canada and the Conference Board. He said a Conservative government would cut income taxes, particularly for the people in the middle and lower income brackets. We are in agreement with that. He said his government would cut sales taxes. We are in agreement in that regard, and they would encourage the provinces to cut their sales taxes as well. Mr. Speaker, I have taken about five minutes to list all the practical things the hon. member took over three hours to outline.
Let me speak about the situation this country finds itself in, keeping in mind the sophistry used by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) during question period today when he referred to the Liberal objective of providing equality of opportunity for the people of Canada. What the Liberal government has done instead since this Prime Minister took office is provide a lack of opportunity for the people of this country.
I am glad to see that the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Sharp) is in his seat today. If my memory serves me correctly, he was the first minister of finance at the time this Prime Minister took office. I want to compare the situation then in April of 1968 with the situation in February of 1978.
In April of 1968 the actual number of unemployed was 375,000 and the actual rate of unemployment was 4.9 per cent of the labour force. In February of 1978, just two months short of the ten years this Prime Minister has been in office, the actual number of unemployed was 1,007,000, and the actual rate of unemployment was 9.5 per cent. In other words, we had an almost threefold increase in the number of unemployed and an increase in the rate of almost 100 per cent.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT AMENDMENT TO EXTEND RANGE OF PERSONS TO WHOM ANTI-INFLATION GUIDELINES APPLY
speechtext: And they call that progress!

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT AMENDMENT TO EXTEND RANGE OF PERSONS TO WHOM ANTI-INFLATION GUIDELINES APPLY
speechtext:
Yes, they call that progress and we are told we are doing quite well in comparison with other countries. The hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan) has informed me that in a news article appearing in the Ottawa Citizen today there is an indication that the rate of unemployment in nine common market countries is 5.9 per cent as compared to the 9.5 per cent in Canada.
In discussing this bill before us today we must consider the history of how we got into this situation and why we are amending a bill we first passed in 1975, more than two years ago. Members will remember that in 1974 the Conservative party, then as now the official opposition, began a campaign across the country calling for a freeze on wages and prices. That was to be a 90 day freeze. That proposal was taken up by the media and given a great deal of prominence. It became an issue in the election campaign of 1974. The Prime Minister of this country travelled across the land from the Atlantic to the

Pacific telling the people of Canada that a freeze on wages and prices would not work, and that the government which he headed would not impose wage controls in this country. The people, particularly the workers in the urban parts, believed the Prime Minister was an honest man. They voted in substantial numbers electing Liberal members while defeating some Conservative and some NDP members of parliament.
We all know that happened in 1975. This Prime Minister, who had won an election on the promise not to impose controls, implemented wage and price controls because, as he said, they were necessary to stop the cost of living from rising. In October 1975 there was sharp inflation, running at an annual rate of 10.5 per cent. After the anti-inflation program was imposed in October of 1975 there was a sharp decrease in the rate. At the end of the first year in which we had controls the cost of living increase had been reduced to 6.2 per cent.
The Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) and the chairman of the Anti-Inflation Board went around flexing their muscles and saying to the people "Look how successful we have been." Some of us tried to warn the government that this to a large extent was an accident and a temporary thing which would not be repeated.
I have not often, if ever, quoted from a speech which I have made in this parliament on an earlier occasion. However, speaking in this House on June 20, 1977 I talked about this question of the cost of living, and I pointed out how in each month from January, 1977 through to June the cost of living had increased by a half to one per cent. I said:
Taking into account the $2 a barrel price increase there will be in July, we are looking at an increase in the cost of living for the year 1977 of between 9 and 10 per cent.
And what happened, Mr. Speaker? We had an increase of exactly 9.5 per cent for the calendar year of 1977. The Minister of Finance is still going around the country arguing that in 1978 the cost of living will only rise by 6 per cent. However, he cannot find a single independent economist in the universities, the business community or anywhere else who will agree with him that such a thing will happen.
The reasons are obvious. First of all, the fall in the Canadian dollar has had a disastrous effect on the cost of living in this country. The business commentator in the Globe and Mail yesterday quoted a speech made recently by David Slater, a member of the Economic Council, in which he quoted from a study done by the Conference Board of comparable wages between the United States and Canada for 1975 which seemed to show that the wage rate in Canada was higher than in the United States. Even if one accepts the validity of that study in 1975, the fact is the dollar in Canada as compared to the dollar in the United States has fallen by 15 cents since 1975. So the Canadian worker has suffered a real decline in the cost of living since this program began.
The second thing is that we have a continuing increase in the cost of energy because the government is committed to staged increases in the cost of oil and natural gas to the
April 5, 1978

consumer until the cost reaches the world price. Thirdly, there has been and continues to be a sharp increase in the cost of food, so much of which is imported from other countries, and which is, therefore, a cost over which we have no control.
The government-I said it then and 1 will say it now, and events have proven me correct-had taken credit for the decline in the rate of inflation through the Anti-Inflation Board. However, when the facts demonstrated that there was no reason to br proud of what was happening, the Anti-Inflation Board suddenly began to try to rationalize matters and deceive the public last October by putting out a booklet called "Kick the Inflation Habit", in which they tried to argue that we were doing quite well. They tried to show that the rate of inflation was continuing to come down. How did they do that? They did that in the classical way of one who wants to lie to the public. They cooked the books. To show how they did it and how they rationalized it, I quote from that pamphlet:
Food, energy and import price movements have obscured somewhat the success that has been attained in reducing the rate of inflation.
Of course, if you take out the major factors for the change in something, then you can prove that the change has not taken place.
What has been the effect of the anti-inflation program? Let us look at it. The program has, in fact, never worked because it has never controlled prices. It has only been successful in the one field in which there was the least reason for implementing it, and that is in controlling and limiting wage increases. Since the program has not worked at all, we believe there is no logic in continuing the program, and for that reason we are going to vote against this bill.
The program has not succeeded in holding down prices, profits or the rate of inflation. All it has done is to hold down the salaries and wages of the low and middle income people. It has been ineffective in controlling executive salaries or the incomes of professionals. The only logic for continuing the program, therefore, is a continuing desire on the part of the government to hold down wages and salaries of the ordinary people of Canada. The government continues to believe that this type of wage increase is the prime cause of inflation when there is all kinds of evidence to indicate that the prime cause is elsewhere altogether. By holding down wages and salaries, the government is restricting the purchasing power of the wage earners, thus holding down consumer demand and lengthening the recession in which we currently find ourselves.
The government has deliberately increased prices on oil products. The oil price increase of last year, this year and the one which will come some months from now will add at least one per cent. It added over one per cent in 1977, and it will add more than one per cent to the over-all cost to the CPI for 1978. For the average family this means approximately $150 a year more to heat a house and drive a car. The oil price increase has contributed to a 15 per cent increase in the price of fuel and utilities in the last year, and we have not yet seen the effect of the latest increase. Moreover, the government is committed to a dollar per barrel increase every six months for the foreseeable future.
Anti-Inflation Act
The cost of buying a house has increased by 9 per cent in the last year for a $50,000 home, which in most cities does not give a person a very elaborate home. This is a price increase of $4,500 and over the average life of a mortgage it is an increase of approximately $12,000. Also the cost of an automobile has risen by nearly 10 per cent in the past 12 months, and recent price stories indicate that the larger car companies will continue to raise their prices in this year. In fact, one has already raised its prices and another has received permission from the AIB for a 5 per cent increase. Food prices in 1977 have gone up by over 15 per cent, and food for home consumption rose by nearly 18 per cent. As a result of all this, we have had an increase over the year in the CPI of 9.5 per cent, and in the last months of 1977 the increase was over 11 per cent.
In spite of this the government, under the provisions of this legislation, is holding down wage increases in the last year of the AIB to 6 per cent. With inflation running at somewhere between 8 and 9 per cent, this means food and energy prices, and even prices of supposedly controlled items are going up at a rate of 9 to 10 per cent a year, and the average person this year will suffer a corresponding decline in his real standard of living.
If they are lucky the average family's income will go up about $900, or $ 18 per week. The average family, if it gets the increase allowed by the AIB, will find its standard of living this year dropping by about $12 per week. For those on fixed income the loss will be even more, about $16 per week for those on fixed incomes of $8,000 per year and about $20 per week for those on fixed incomes of $10,000 per year. What we have always needed is an alternative to the anti-inflation board, a plan that protects those on low and fixed incomes and guarantees the purchasing power of ordinary people so that we can begin to work our way out of the combined recession and inflation that has characterized this country for the past few years.
We have been told that the reason we had inflation was that workers were demanding and getting too high wage increases. I refer now to the period in 1975 when the government brought its program in. What the government conveniently forgot to tell people was that in 1975 workers were reacting to the very sharp increases in profits which Canadian corporations had been able to achieve in the years 1972 to 1974. Profits more than doubled in those three years. It was very natural for workers to try to get their share of the increased productivity and the increased gross national product of this country.
We were told that we needed the anti-inflation program to protect our markets. Although we have had the controls and although the wage demands of Canadian workers were restricted, what we have had is complete disaster. Our major export products, such as metals, have not been selling, not because the price was wrong but to a large extent because the market was not good. There has been a world recession. They have not been selling because our very patriotic multinational

April 5, 1978
Anti-Inflation Act
corporations such as International Nickel found it wise from their point of view, wise from the point of view of their management, wise from the point of view of their shareholders, but disastrous for their workers, to take the profits they made in Canada and the loans so generously provided by this government and invest that money in mines in Indonesia and Guatemala. These mines compete for sales with Canadian mines and for jobs with Canadian workers.
In a fit of honesty-not found too often-a senior Inco official admitted and later retracted, I am sure under a great deal of pressure, that of course Inco could not conceive of cutting back production in Indonesia or Guatemala because those governments simply would not permit it. Only in a country like Canada with a supine government such as we have could this take place.
When I began I said that our actual rate of unemployment today is 9V4 per cent. Is that temporary, Mr. Speaker? Is it likely to go away in the near future? Is it likely to improve? There is not a single reason to believe that is likely to happen.
The current issue of Macleans, Mr. Speaker, should have been paid for, if it was not, by the Liberal party because it is an out-and-out propaganda pamphlet for that party. It contains an article by Ian Urquhart entitled "What Price Trudeau? If he didn't hurt the Economy, he sure didn't help it." Then there are four "report cards" given by four economists who were asked to rate the Prime Minister. I should like to quote a couple of sentences each from three of them.
The first one is by John F. Helliwell, Department of Economics, University of British Columbia, and has the heading "Trudeau's Report Card No. 1: A very Average Student". The text reads as follows:
GRADE: C
The student was asked to find and implement policies that would achieve reasonably full employment, reasonably stable prices, efficient, innovative and peaceful operation of the public and private sectors, and less disparity of income and opportunity across the country. The student failed the exam ...
Carl Beigie, C. D. Howe Research Institute, Montreal under the heading "Trudeau's Report Card No. 2: Not working to Potential", writes as follows:
GRADE: C
Mr. Trudeau inherited two major economic problems when he became Prime Minister-regional disparities and a weak international competitive position in most manufactured products. Both are now even more serious.
The last one I want to quote is Professor J. C. Weldon, Department of Economics, McGill University. Under the heading "Trudeau's Report Card No. 4: Should seek other Work", he writes:
GRADE: F
Not deserved? Perhaps, but it is the lowest grade the rules allow. I suppose the principal charge to be laid against the Trudeau government is that it has adopted the most reactionary of all economic policies, namely to abandon policy. The vital commitment of 1945 to full employment has vanished.
In case members on the government side think that I am being much too partisan and being unrealistic in speaking about full employment, let me remind them of a white paper published by a Liberal government in 1945. One of the great

men in the Liberal history of this country, C. D. Howe, was minister of reconstruction. When tabling the white paper he said that the central task of reconstruction was to maintain a high and stable level of employment and income, a task the government adopted as a primary objective of policy. He said that government was not thereby selecting a lower target than full employment.
That was the commitment of the Liberal government in 1945 and we must compare that with the record in February, 1978 when over one million were unemployed and 9.5 per cent of the labour force was out of work and looking for work. We know that is an under-estimation of the actual number of unemployed. We know that there are several hundred thousand-probably 500,000 people-who have given up looking for work because it is no use, there is no work in the areas in which they live.
Our party believes in 1978, as did the Liberal government in 1945, that full employment is both necessary and possible. We believe that and we say it can be done. Indeed, we know it can be done. If we are to achieve that goal, however, we must order our system much better than we have been doing.
In a recent report on industrial policy the Science Council of Canada gave as one of the major causes of our economic turndown the fractionalization of industry because of the high degree of foreign ownership in our manufacturing sector and our subservience through branch plant organization to investment decisions being made by large foreign industrial concerns. Mr. Speaker, is there a member of this House from any party who would not agree with that assessment? Is it not obvious that our branch plants are not able and interested in providing the jobs which are necessary?
We have in many fields an efficient industry productivity. In the Canadian steel industry it has always been high. Output of the worker increased by 6 per cent between 1975 and 1976. Canadian steel prices are 10 per cent to 20 per cent lower than that of comparable American products. We are able to sell 70 per cent of our steel exports to the United States and yet the employment rate has been falling in that industry. While we are not exporters of steel, we run a deficit in imported manufactured goods incorporating steel. These manufactured goods are auto parts, aircraft parts, agricultural implements, appliances, machinery and equipment. The biggest drawback to expansion in this industry is weak demand. As a result there are less people employed this year than there were in earlier years.
Those of us who were here in parliament at the time when the auto pact was negotiated remember the glowing promises made by the then minister of industry, Mr. Drury, about how we were to get a better share of the automobile market, how we were to get more skilled jobs, how we would get lower prices for cars. Mr. Speaker, we have more jobs but the skilled jobs are in the United States. The assembly jobs are available in Canada. The tool and die makers are in the United States. We have not developed a tool and die industry. We have let
April 5, 1978

our electronics industry and our television industry go. What we have had is a series of plant closures and layoffs.
Let me put on the record just a few of them. RCA is getting out of the major appliance business. CAMCO, formerly West-inghouse, manufacturer of dishwashers, refrigerators and ranges, has reduced employment from a high of 1,400 in 1973 to the present 700. Appliances, formerly made in Barrie by Canadian General Electric, are now being shipped in from the parent plant in the United States. These products include vacuum cleaners, electric knives, hair dryers, deep fryers, blenders, food processors, etc. The workers at CGE in Peterborough attribute the drop in employment from a high of 4,500 to 3,000 in 1975 and to the present low of 2,300 to the depressed economy and the fact that the company has been moving many sections of its operations elsewhere. I could go on and on.
We may not know it because the GATT negotiators have not said so publicly, but what we gather and are told by people in the industry is that our negotiators are prepared, if they can get some more concessions for tariff reductions on raw materials such as minerals and lumber, which we export, to agree to substantial tariff cuts for manufactured goods coming into Canada. That means fewer jobs and more unemployment in Canada.
Having damned the government's program and having indicated how miserably the anti-inflation program has failed,
I want to take the few moments remaining to me to put on the record the concrete steps which we think should be followed by a Canadian government.
First of all, there must be a real commitment to full employment. This country can and must have full employment. It must offer to every Canadian citizen who is able and willing to work a meaningful job. How can that be accomplished? We believe that our monetary and fiscal policies must be timed adjusted and implemented to attain this objective. We believe that our manpower policies and training programs should be developed and co-ordinated to bring jobs and people together. That obviously has not been done. Publications such as the Financial Post are predicting that we will have a very serious shortage of skilled craftsmen despite the fact that we have spent billions of dollars on our manpower training programs. We believe that substantial moneys should be allotted by all levels of government for programs to create jobs providing decent living wages. What we have had instead, despite the urging of the official opposition, is the exact reverse-restraint and cutbacks. These have meant more unemployment in all provinces of Canada.
We believe that we need a massive low income housing program to help solve the severe housing shortage and, as well, to provide jobs. We believe an industrial strategy must be developed which would promote and create secondary manufacturing, provide long-range solutions to energy problems, deal with manpower needs, transportation, housing and land use, and concentrate on employment. We believe that there must be a redistribution of income in this country. We must face up to the fact that the present Minister of National
Anti-Inflation Act
Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) stated so clearly in her recent speech, namely that in more than 30 years income distribution in Canada has hardly changed at all. Where it has changed, it has changed for the worse. Thirty years ago the lowest 20 per cent of income earners of this country got about 4 per cent of the gross national product. The top 20 per cent received more than ten times that. They got 42.5 per cent of the gross national product. Thirty years later according to the latest figures, the bottom 20 per cent get 3.9 per cent and the top 20 per cent get 44 per cent of the gross national product.
What should we do about income redistribution? First of all, we should scrap the Anti-Inflation Board since its main thrust has been to keep down wages and not prices. Secondly, the tax system should be restructured to be more equitable. Thirdly, those on the lower end of the income scale should have their personal income taxes lowered and the sales taxes should be cut. Fourthly, pensioners and those on fixed incomes should have their purchasing power restored by tax adjustments and by increasing benefits. Lastly, real taxes on corporation profits should be increased.
I have tried to sketch not just what is wrong with the government's program but what a government that is really concerned about the welfare of this country should do. This government has failed lamentably, Mr. Speaker. It has not met the needs of the Canadian people. One of the most dramatic ways of indicating that feeling is to vote against this bill, because this program has been a complete failure. For those reasons, we intend to vote against this bill.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT AMENDMENT TO EXTEND RANGE OF PERSONS TO WHOM ANTI-INFLATION GUIDELINES APPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have already made a contribution to this debate on this patch-up bill, C-18, but I want to put in a few final remarks at this time. I do not want members on the other side to think we are holding things up over here. I know they have had a lot of information given to them by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) but I would refer the House to the fact that the bill had only two days of debate in the House earlier before it was referred to the Standing committee, where it received speedy passage after only four committee meetings. I would also stress that we in the opposition are going to be consistent and stick to our position in opposing this kind of bill.
I think it is interesting, though, to refer to the draft bill which my hon. friend from York-Simcoe mentioned in his remarks. I have the draft bill here in my hand, a discussion draft bearing the name of D. Maurais from the Department of Justice, legislation branch. It makes reference to the minister as being the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). It is interesting that at our last committee meeting on March 16 the minister said to the committee in reference to this bill, which he said he saw for the first time in the committee:
It has never been government policy and I have never seen it before. It was shown to me by a member of the opposition and I denied that day and I deny today that we had any intention whatever to present such a bill.
Now that is a fairly straightforward statement, but I have to go back a little further to February 17 when we were also in

April 5, 1978
Anti-Inflation Act
committee and the minister, again referring to the bill, said this:
I have never approved and do not have any intention to approve; I do not intend to put it in front of my colleagues in cabinet. I have said that to the unions, I said it to the businessmen and I now say it to the premiers. There was no such thing. How could I say more?
He was referring again to that bill. I commented that this was reassuring and at that same meeting-I am quoting myself here-I said:
If the Economic Council would not take on the job there would be legislation?
To which the minister replied: "For a monitoring agency, yes". The minister said he did not want to see the bill and continued:
You know, Mr. Stevens presented it. He had the bill in his hand. I have never seen such a bill. My name is on it, but I have never seen it.
I thought it was poor that we should have the minister at the meeting without having the advantage of having seen such a bill, so on the next occasion, also at a meeting of the finance committee, I reminded him that on Friday I had said that I would try to get a copy of it for him. I said I had it with me, but the minister said: "I do not want to see it." He did not want to see it even though he had been reminded that his name was on it. Subsequently the minister was asked by me who Mr. Maurais was, the one who had drafted the bill, and the minister said he did not know who that was. Finally, at this same meeting, I asked the minister whether he would undertake for the benefit of the committee to determine where this bill originated, who drafted it, under whose authority, and why it was released. I said:
Mr. Chairman, I said I was willing to obtain a copy and I did obtain a copy for the minister but he does not want it.
The minister said: "It was given to me here. I will take it home." So finally, on February 17, we have the minister admitting that he has the copy and that he will take it home even though some weeks later he says in the same committee:
I have never seen it before it was shown to me. And I denied that day and I deny today that we have any intention whatever to present such a bill.
That is very strange, Mr. Speaker, and in order to try and clarify as to how this draft bill came into being, I decided we had better ask a question in the House about it. Accordingly, on February 22 I put a question to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) because, after all, legislation does emanate from the Department of Justice. I asked him whether he would tell us who in his office had instructed Mr. D. Maurais to draft this bill and who had authorized the release of the bill across the country. Now that is a fairly straightforward question. At that time the minister said simply that he did not know the name of the officer and added "I would have to find out who he is in order to ascertain from whom he received his instructions."
That was approximately six weeks ago and we have not yet had an answer from the Minister of Justice with regard to that question. I tried to catch Your Honour's eye today so that I could refresh his memory on this matter. I am assured by the minister that he will have an answer for the House tomorrow. I regret he did not have it available before now but I would remind the House, since I will not have an opportunity to do so

tomorrow, that the name of D. Maurais is the ninth name on the list of some 14 officers in the legislative section of the Department of Justic. He is listed right here in the government of Canada telephone book and if the minister has any trouble finding him I will be glad to help.
Leaving that mystery aside for the moment I should like to deal with the issue of restraint. Ministers have assured us they are anxious to exercise restraint, yet the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras), when presenting the estimates this year, took great pleasure from the fact that the government was reducing the rate of increase in public expenditure. He did not say that expenditures were down or that the government had been able to hold the line with regard to expenditure. No, the only thing the minister could take credit for was a reduction in the rate of increase.
We cannot afford to carry on this kind of spending spiral. We have to do something more serious than having the rate of spending increase going down. Of course, as the hon. member for York-Simcoe has said, it is really all a matter of confidence in the economy; but I must say that if one looks at the record of the government one cannot escape the conviction that the record is not an impressive one. How can we have confidence in a government led by a prime minister who said to us some time ago that inflation had been wrestled to the ground and that separatism in Canada was dead?
I have a couple of quotations here from recent magazines. This is the same man who in July, 1974 said:
You cannot start with a policy and then run away from it every time you want to get a new sector of the population to support you.
Well, we have seen some of the changes of mind of the government opposite and if they have any shred of consistency left, it is this: when they get a bad policy they sure stick to it. I guess this is why we have a bad record on unemployment and inflation.
Another couple of quotes from the leader of the government party. Here is one from December, 1975. He does not like the system the way it is. He says:
We haven't been able to make it work, the free market system. We've ended up with very high unemployment and very high inflation. We can't go back to what was before with the same habits, the same behaviour and the same institutions. Otherwise, we'd be back to high unemployment and high inflation ... That means the government is going to take a larger role in running institutions.
That was two and a half years ago, and since the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made that statement we have had nothing but high unemployment, high inflation and a government which takes a larger and larger role in running institutions. If the government cannot learn from its mistakes, I do not know how we can expect it to change the direction in which Canada is going or to increase confidence in Canada.
If we think the statements of the Prime Minister are strange, perhaps we ought to compare his statements with the actions of his government. In the 1974 election campaign the government campaigned against controls of any kind and made a mockery of the temporary freeze proposed by the
April 5, 1978

Conservative party. Then, as we all know, 15 months later the government imposed a 39-month program of controls. Can we believe what the government says?
In that same 1974 election campaign the government promised the residents of Toronto a $30 million waterfront park. Well, the residents of Toronto know that nothing has happened on that score. That is another example of this government changing its mind.
The government promised other cities aid in the form of grants for rapid transit systems, but every mayor in the country can tell us that there has been no money for rapid transit since that election promise in 1974. I suppose we should not be too surprised at the actions of the government opposite.
I see that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) is here. I appreciate the fact that he is listening attentively because I want to refer to some of his problems. He tells the country quite blithely that his department does not have any deficit. The fact that it spends something like $1.7 billion more than it takes in is, in the words of the minister, a commitment of the government. I hope the minister can sell that to the taxpayers, particularly those who are either selfemployed or who are retired and do not contribute to or benefit from the unemployment insurance scheme, but who, nevertheless, are required to pick up their share of the tab through general taxation. Some insurance scheme!
I remember that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) told the country about the great things his department was going to do, but we find that there was such a small increase in national defence spending that it did not even keep up with the rate of inflation.
If the voters of the country can be forgiven for wondering about the practices of the government opposite, I wonder how the voters of Vancouver feel. Every time many of my constituents look out of their windows in the morning they can see 13 to 15 ocean-going ships anchored in the harbour. Why are they anchored in the harbour? They are waiting for grain. Where is the grain? The grain is out on the prairies because the government cannot get it to Vancouver to ship it to the people who want it, the Russians or the Chinese. Who pays the cost of these ships waiting around in Vancouver harbour, and who is at fault? At the very least the taxpayer pays. Farmers probably pay more than other taxpayers do. We know where the fault lies. No one can take the blame except the government opposite.
Let us go back to the time when the government told farmers that they should not grow anything because the government could not sell it. Farmers were going to be paid for not producing. Now they are told to produce as much as they can, even though it cannot be shipped out.
What are the results of this lack of planning and leadership on the part of the government? Recently we have seen a flight of capital from Canada, principally to the United States because that country is so close to us. That is not really surprising. Any time a government creates a hostile environment for people or capital, they leave. We need only examine
Anti-Inflation Act
the situation in Quebec at the present time under its separatist government. That government has frightened many people and undermined confidence in that province. Many companies and individuals are leaving Quebec because of the hostile environment there. We had the same problem in British Columbia a few years ago when we had an NDP government. One result of policies which are unfriendly to businesses and individuals is that there is a tendency to save money rather than to invest. Another result is higher unemployment because the private sector will not invest in order to create the jobs which are needed.
It is really a shame to see Canadian expertise and Canadian money going to the United States to provide housing for American citizens. The Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) tells us we have a housing crisis in Canada. We do not have a housing crisis; we have a money crisis. Many people cannot afford the houses that are available. There are empty units all over Canada. Units financed by the government opposite are competing with private sector units, and some government financed units are even competing with other government financed units. It is ludicrous that the government should be competing with itself. In some small centres apartment units financed under the National Housing Act by CMHC are competing with new houses built under AHOP. The result is that people invest in housing for themselves only. What we really need is more investment in housing and in other industries in order to get things going again.
Finally, I want to conclude this fairly short intervention by saying that it is extremely unfortunate for the country and for the confidence that taxpayers are expected to have when government ministers-and I have just illustrated a few cases-do not even know what is going on in their own departments. We cannot expect to have confidence until hon. ministers opposite can show that they know what is going on in their departments and that they are interested in what is happening. When the government has no idea-as illustrated by the quotations I have cited-of what direction it should take, it runs for cover because it knows it has to take care of itself; and if it does not know what direction the country should take and the effects of its policies on the whole economy, the results can be devastating indeed.

subtopic: ANTI-INFLATION ACT AMENDMENT TO EXTEND RANGE OF PERSONS TO WHOM ANTI-INFLATION GUIDELINES APPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as we approach the beginning of the dismantling of controls on April 14, 1 think we should take a look at the problems we will have to handle in a satisfactory way if we are to avoid a recurrence of the situation which made the imposition of controls necessary in the first place.
First of all, we must realize that human nature does not change very much from year to year and that the impulses and desires which caused management, labour and government to act in the way they did prior to the imposition of controls in 1975 will still be about the same when controls are lifted. Knowing this, in what way can we expect these three components of society to react when the economy becomes free of controls once again?

April 5, 1978
Anti-Inflation Act
We can expect organized labour to put forward demands for the accumulated wage increases it considers were wrongly denied it by the AIB during the period when controls were in force.
We can expect management to give in to labour's demands for wage increases rather than risk work stoppages and the consequent loss of profits, as it did in most cases during the period which preceded the imposition of controls. These wage increases will, once again, be passed on to the buying public in the form of higher prices. Management can also be expected to resume the practice of charging what it considers the traffic will bear in order to obtain the best possible return for its shareholders.
We can expect government to continue spending far in excess of what can be justified by proper management of its responsibilities to the public and to be the worst offender of all in fueling the fires of inflation.
Realizing that there will be sharp upward pressures on wages and prices as soon as controls are lifted, the government has announced guidelines, and has asked the Economic Council of Canada to monitor our price and wage performance after controls have been removed. Now, how effective will this monitoring mechanism be? The best way to arrive at an answer to that question is to see what success a similar approach to controlling wage and price rises had when it was tried some years ago.
In June, 1969 the government established the Prices and Incomes Commission under the chairmanship of Dr. John Young in an attempt to control price and wage increases. Soon after it came into being, the commission announced price and wage guidelines to be followed by management and labour, and started to monitor price and wage performances.
As wages kept on rising at an unacceptable rate, the commission brought this to the attention of the unions concerned, and strongly urged that the government's guidelines be obeyed. The unions paid no attention to the commission, because it had no powers to compel compliance with the guidelines. As wages continued to rise, prices also continued to go up at an unacceptable rate. Management's reply to the commission was that these price increases were necessary to compensate for the wage increases that were taking place, and so the price-wage spiral continued unchecked.
It became obvious that without the provision of teeth to require compliance with the guidelines, the commission was powerless to control or even slow down price and wage increases, and it finally went out of existence in June, 1972, a very disappointing failure.
When those of us who were around here ten years ago hear the government announcing guidelines, to be monitored by a mechanism that will have no power to require compliance with the guidelines, we get the very definite feeling that "this is where we came in". There is no reason for believing that the government's proposed method of getting labour and management to comply with its guidelines after April 14 will be any less of a failure than it was between 1969 and 1972. To try to pretend that the present approach will be any more successful than it was then is a blatant attempt to mislead the people of this country.
And, of course, that is exactly what the present plan is. April 14 will be very close to the day when the election will be called, and the vote will be in the latter part of June. The government's plan is for very gradual decontrol in the early stages, which means that very little decontrolling will have taken place before the end of June. This plan will, of course, give the government the best of both worlds. It will please those voters who are clamouring for decontrol, and sharp increases in prices will not become apparent until after the election is over.
In addition to our own buying capabilities, why is it so necessary to keep our price levels from rising at an excessive rate? The main reason for applying controls in 1975 was that rapidly accelerating inflation was making our products less and less competitive in both the Canadian and the export market, and production and employment were adversely affected. In this regard, we are particularly vulnerable to price levels in the United States, the country which is by far our most important trading partner and with whom we do 70 per cent of our export and import business. Neither Americans nor Canadians are willing to pay more for a Canadian product if they can buy a similar American product at a lower price.
For many months now, prices in the United States have been rising less rapidly than ours, and that is one of the principal reasons why our production and unemployment have been steadily worsening. If this spread between our price levels grows even greater, our loss of orders to the United States will be even greater than at present, and unemployment in Canada will increase at an even faster rate than during recent months.
The complete failure experienced by the Prices and Incomes Commission in trying to control price and wage increases without the power to compel management and labour to obey the government's guidelines shows the futility of a monitoring mechanism without teeth to require compliance with the guidelines. I believe that the teeth which are required are for the government to say, very clearly, that if inflation due to causes generated within our economy rises for two successive quarters at an annual rate greater than 1 per cent above the annual rate at the time when decontrol starts, controls will be reimposed.
Past experience has demonstrated that without such teeth we will be heading for failure before we even start and will have inflation which will accelerate more rapidly than that which made controls necessary in the first place.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock?
